decks.domain: Handling emergencies: avoiding crashes, what to do after a crash, when a crash must be reported, and roadside vehicle failures

cards.front: What is the first step in an emergency where someone is hurt?
cards.back: In any emergency where you or someone else is hurt, the first step is to call nine one one.

cards.front: Are most crashes avoidable, and what helps you avoid one?
cards.back: Most crashes can be avoided, and paying close attention to your surroundings helps you choose the right way to avoid one.

cards.front: What happens to a teen driver's crash risk with another teen in the car?
cards.back: A teen driver's chance of a crash doubles when another teen is riding in the vehicle.

cards.front: How do you warn drivers behind you about a vehicle on the side of the road?
cards.back: When you spot a vehicle on the side of the road, warn drivers behind you by tapping your brake pedal three or four times.

cards.front: Is tapping the brake three or four times a way to stop in an emergency?
cards.back: Tapping the brake three or four times is a warning signal to drivers behind you, not an emergency stopping method.
cards.memory_hook: Taps warn; they do not stop

cards.front: What are the three ways the handbook gives to try to avoid a crash?
cards.back: The handbook gives three ways to try to avoid a crash: stop, turn or speed up.

decks.domain: Handling emergencies: avoiding crashes, what to do after a crash, when a crash must be reported, and roadside vehicle failures

cards.front: How do you make a fast emergency stop with ABS?
cards.back: To stop fast with ABS, press the brake pedal firmly and keep steady pressure until you have stopped or the danger is over.

cards.front: What does ABS do when you brake?
cards.back: ABS keeps the wheels from locking when you brake, so you can stop with little or no skidding.

cards.front: Should you pump the pedal during an ABS emergency stop?
cards.back: Emergency braking with ABS uses firm, continuous pressure, not repeated pumping of the pedal.

cards.front: What risk comes with stopping quickly?
cards.back: Stopping quickly can lead a driver behind you to crash into you, so keep track of the vehicles behind.

cards.front: If you turn to avoid a crash, how should you hold the wheel, and why stay ready?
cards.back: If you turn to avoid a crash, hold the wheel firmly with both hands and be ready to keep control afterward, since some drivers dodge one collision only to cause another.

cards.front: Is dodging one collision the whole job when you turn away?
cards.back: Turning away from one collision is only half the job, because you must then keep control so you do not cause a second one.

cards.front: When steering away from danger, where should you steer?
cards.back: When steering away from danger, always steer where you want the vehicle to go and never into the oncoming lane.
cards.memory_hook: Steer where you want, never oncoming

cards.front: When can speeding up be the best escape?
cards.back: Speeding up can be the best escape when another vehicle is about to strike your car from the side or the rear, and you slow down again once the danger has passed.

cards.front: What is the handbook's example of when to speed up, and what do you do after?
cards.back: The handbook example for speeding up is a vehicle about to strike your car from the side or the rear, and you slow down again once that danger has passed.

decks.domain: Handling emergencies: avoiding crashes, what to do after a crash, when a crash must be reported, and roadside vehicle failures

cards.front: After a crash, when should you stay at the scene, and how do you warn others?
cards.back: If you are involved in a crash, or emergency help has not yet arrived, stay at the scene and warn other drivers with your emergency flashers or flares.

cards.front: If someone is injured or killed, what three things do you do at the scene?
cards.back: If someone is injured or killed, call nine one one, stay at the scene without moving the vehicles, and stay inside your vehicle if that is safe.

cards.front: Is leaving the scene of an injury crash allowed?
cards.back: Leaving the scene of a crash in which someone is injured or killed is a crime.

cards.front: If no one is hurt but your car cannot move, what do you do?
cards.back: If no one is hurt but your vehicle cannot be moved, call nine one one, follow the dispatcher's directions and stay away from traffic.

cards.front: If no one is hurt and your car can move, what should you do?
cards.back: If no one is hurt and your vehicle can move, drive it off the road when safe rather than blocking traffic or stopping in the middle of the road.

cards.front: How does the stuck-car case differ from the drivable-car case when no one is hurt?
cards.back: With no injuries but a car that cannot move, you call nine one one, follow the directions given and stay away from traffic, whereas a drivable car is moved off the road.

cards.front: How does handling the vehicles differ between an injury crash and a minor one?
cards.back: With an injury or death you leave the vehicles where they are, but with no injuries and a drivable car you move it off the road.

cards.front: What information do you collect from other drivers after a crash?
cards.back: After a crash, collect each other driver's license, vehicle and insurance information.

cards.front: What else should you record after a crash?
cards.back: Also record the damage to every vehicle, write down how the crash happened and get contact information from any witnesses.

decks.domain: Handling emergencies: avoiding crashes, what to do after a crash, when a crash must be reported, and roadside vehicle failures

cards.front: When must every crash with people hurt be reported to police?
cards.back: A crash must be reported to police whenever someone is injured or killed.

cards.front: At what amount of property damage must a crash be reported?
cards.back: A crash must be reported to police when property damage reaches one thousand dollars or more.

cards.front: At what amount of government property damage must a crash be reported?
cards.back: A crash must be reported to police when damage to government property, such as signs or guardrails, reaches two hundred dollars or more.

cards.front: How do the two dollar thresholds for reporting compare?
cards.back: The police reporting threshold is one thousand dollars for property damage in general but only two hundred dollars for damage to government property such as signs or guardrails.

cards.front: Which other two situations require a police report?
cards.back: A crash must also be reported to police when your vehicle cannot be moved or a driver seems to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

cards.front: Can a crash with no injuries still need a police report?
cards.back: A crash needs a police report even without injuries or major damage when a vehicle cannot be moved or a driver appears impaired.

decks.domain: Handling emergencies: avoiding crashes, what to do after a crash, when a crash must be reported, and roadside vehicle failures

cards.front: In a roadside emergency, what two things do you do first?
cards.back: In a roadside emergency, call nine one one if anyone is injured and turn on your emergency flashers.

cards.front: What should you do if your brakes stop working?
cards.back: If your brakes stop working, pump the brake pedal several times and then pull the parking brake.

cards.front: What if pulling the parking brake starts a skid?
cards.back: If using the parking brake starts a skid, release it, and look for a safe place to slow to a stop.

cards.front: What is the order of steps when the brakes fail?
cards.back: When the brakes fail, pumping the pedal comes first and the parking brake second, and the parking brake is released if it causes a skid.

cards.front: What should you do after a tire blowout?
cards.back: After a tire blowout, hold the steering wheel to keep going straight, lift your foot off the gas, slow down gradually and pull off the road when safe.

cards.front: What should you do if the engine quits?
cards.back: If the engine quits, hold the wheel, leave the key in the on position and pull to the side when safe, expecting the steering to be hard to turn.

cards.front: Why expect extra effort steering after the engine stops?
cards.back: The handbook warns that the steering wheel will be hard to turn after the engine stops, so expect extra effort while pulling over.

cards.front: What should you do if your headlights stop working?
cards.back: If your headlights stop working, try switching them off and on in case only the parking lights were on, turn on the emergency flashers and pull off the road when safe.

cards.front: What should you do if the gas pedal sticks?
cards.back: If the gas pedal sticks, keep your eyes on the road, shift into neutral, pull off the road when safe and then turn off the engine.

cards.front: When the engine dies, do you turn the key off?
cards.back: When the engine dies you keep the key in the on position, and only with a stuck gas pedal does the handbook say to turn the engine off, once you are safely off the road.

cards.front: How does handling a stuck gas pedal differ from a blowout?
cards.back: A stuck gas pedal is handled by shifting into neutral, while a blowout is handled by easing off the gas and slowing gradually.

recap_hooks.text: When someone is hurt, call for emergency help first.
Most crashes can be avoided by paying close attention.
Tap your brakes to warn drivers behind you, and remember: stop, turn or speed up.
With ABS, press firmly and hold steady pressure.
Turning away means both hands, steering where you want, and never into oncoming traffic.
Speed up for a threat from the side or rear, then slow down.
Stay at the scene and warn others with flashers or flares.
With injuries, leave the vehicles in place; leaving the scene is a crime.
Exchange license, vehicle and insurance information and record what happened.
Report injury or death crashes to police.
Report property damage of one thousand dollars, or two hundred for government property.
Also report when a car cannot move or a driver seems impaired.
Failed brakes: pump, then the parking brake, released if it skids.
Blowout: hold straight and ease off; engine stops: key on and pull over.
Stuck pedal: neutral, pull off, then turn off the engine.
